chapters.title: The ascension and a replacement for Judas

parts.text: The risen Jesus shows himself alive over forty days and teaches about God’s kingdom. He tells the apostles to wait in Jerusalem for the promised Holy Ghost, who will empower their witness from Jerusalem to the ends of the earth. Asked about restoring Israel’s kingdom, he leaves the times in the Father’s authority. Jesus is taken up into a cloud, and two men in white promise that he will return in the same manner. The disciples return to Jerusalem and continue together in prayer.

Among about 120 disciples, Peter explains Judas’s betrayal and death through the Psalms and calls for another witness to join the apostles. The replacement must have accompanied Jesus’ ministry from John’s baptism through the ascension and testify to his resurrection. After two candidates are proposed and the group prays for God’s choice, the lot falls to Matthias, who joins the eleven.

On Pentecost, a sound like rushing wind fills the house, tongues like fire appear, and the believers speak in other languages as the Holy Ghost enables them. Visitors hear God’s wonderful works in their native tongues. Peter explains the event through Joel’s promise of the Spirit. He proclaims that the crucified Jesus has risen, citing David’s words about resurrection and exaltation. The apostles witness to this, and the outpoured Spirit shows that God has made Jesus both Lord and Christ.

Convicted hearers ask what to do. Peter calls them to repent and be baptized in Jesus Christ’s name for remission of sins, promising the Holy Ghost to those God calls. About three thousand receive the word and are baptized. They devote themselves to apostolic teaching, fellowship, breaking bread, and prayer. Believers share possessions to meet needs, worship gladly, and see the Lord adding to the church daily.

At the temple’s Beautiful gate, a man lame from birth asks Peter and John for money. Peter has no silver or gold but commands him in Jesus Christ’s name to rise and walk. Taking his hand, Peter raises him, and his feet and ankles become strong. He enters the temple walking, leaping, and praising God, astonishing people who recognize the familiar beggar.

Peter tells the gathered crowd that their own power or holiness did not heal him; faith in the risen Jesus did. Though the people and rulers rejected the Prince of life in ignorance, God fulfilled the prophets’ announcement of Christ’s suffering. Peter calls for repentance and conversion, speaking of forgiveness, refreshing, and the promised restoration. Jesus is the prophet Moses commanded them to hear and the fulfilment of God’s covenant blessing, sent first to turn them from their sins.

The authorities arrest Peter and John for preaching resurrection through Jesus, but many believe. Before the council, Peter declares that the healed man stands through Jesus Christ, whom they crucified and God raised. Salvation is found in no other name. The leaders recognize the apostles’ association with Jesus and cannot deny the healing. They threaten them and forbid further preaching, but Peter and John answer that they must speak what they have seen and heard.

The believers pray together, relating opposition to the Psalms and God’s purpose. They ask for boldness and for healing and signs in Jesus’ name. Their meeting place shakes, and they are filled with the Holy Ghost and speak boldly. The community shares resources so no one lacks, while the apostles powerfully testify to the resurrection. Barnabas sells land and places its proceeds at the apostles’ feet.

Ananias and Sapphira sell property, secretly retain part, and present their gift deceitfully. Peter explains that the property and money were theirs to control, but they have lied to God. Each dies after the deception is exposed, bringing great fear on the church. Meanwhile, signs and wonders accompany the apostles, believers increase, and crowds bring sick and afflicted people who are healed.

Jealous leaders imprison the apostles, but an angel releases them and sends them back to teach in the temple. Before the council they insist on obeying God rather than men and testify to the risen, exalted Jesus. Gamaliel urges caution: a human movement will fail, but opposing God’s work would mean fighting God. The apostles are beaten and forbidden to preach, yet rejoice to suffer for Jesus’ name and continue teaching daily.

As disciples multiply, Grecian believers complain that their widows are neglected in the daily distribution. The twelve ask the community to choose seven men of good reputation, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, to oversee this responsibility while the apostles devote themselves to prayer and the word. Stephen, Philip, and five others are chosen and commissioned with prayer and laying on of hands. The word spreads, disciples increase, and many priests obey the faith.

Stephen performs great wonders and speaks with wisdom his opponents cannot resist. They secretly arrange accusations of blasphemy and stir up the people and leaders. Brought before the council, he faces false witnesses claiming he attacks the temple and law and says Jesus will change Moses’ customs. Those watching see his face appear like an angel’s.

Stephen recounts God’s dealings with Israel, from Abraham’s call and promises to Joseph’s rejection and exaltation in Egypt. He describes Moses’ preservation, initial rejection by his brethren, divine calling at the burning bush, and leadership in delivering Israel. The rejected Moses became their appointed ruler and foretold another prophet they must hear. Yet the fathers resisted him, turned toward Egypt, and worshipped idols, bringing judgment.

Stephen recalls the tabernacle and Solomon’s temple while affirming that the Creator cannot be confined to handmade buildings. He charges his hearers with continuing their fathers’ resistance to the Holy Ghost: they have betrayed and killed the Just One and failed to keep the law. Enraged, they drag him out and stone him as he sees Jesus standing at God’s right hand. Stephen asks Jesus to receive his spirit and forgive his killers; Saul watches over their clothes.

chapters.title: The gospel in Samaria and on the road

parts.text: Persecution after Stephen’s death scatters believers from Jerusalem, and Saul imprisons men and women. Those scattered preach the word. Philip’s preaching and miracles bring joy and belief in Samaria, including the belief and baptism of Simon, formerly a sorcerer. Peter and John come, pray, and lay hands on the believers, who receive the Holy Ghost. Simon offers money for this authority, but Peter rebukes the idea that God’s gift can be purchased and calls him to repent.

An angel directs Philip toward Gaza, where the Spirit leads him to an Ethiopian official reading Esaias. Beginning with the passage about the suffering figure led like a lamb to slaughter, Philip preaches Jesus. The official confesses faith in Jesus Christ as God’s Son and is baptized. The Spirit carries Philip away; the official continues rejoicing, while Philip preaches from Azotus toward Cesarea.

On his way to arrest believers in Damascus, Saul encounters a heavenly light and hears Jesus asking why he persecutes him. Blinded, Saul is led into the city. The Lord sends Ananias, explaining that Saul is chosen to bear his name before Gentiles, kings, and Israel and will suffer for him. Saul regains sight, is baptized, and begins preaching Jesus as God’s Son. He escapes a murder plot in a basket. Barnabas introduces him to Jerusalem’s wary disciples, but renewed threats send him to Tarsus. The churches enjoy peace and growth.

At Lydda, Peter tells the bedridden Eneas that Jesus Christ heals him, and the healing turns many to the Lord. In Joppa, the generous disciple Tabitha dies. Peter comes, prays, and calls her to rise, presenting her alive to the believers and widows. Many believe, and Peter stays with Simon the tanner.

An angel tells the devout centurion Cornelius to send for Peter. Meanwhile Peter sees a sheet of animals and hears a command to eat, followed by the warning not to call unclean what God has cleansed. The Spirit directs him to accompany Cornelius’s messengers. At Cesarea, Peter refuses Cornelius’s worship and explains that God has taught him not to call any person common or unclean. Cornelius describes his vision, and the assembled household waits to hear God’s message.

Peter declares God’s impartiality and recounts Jesus’ ministry, death, and resurrection. Jesus is appointed judge of the living and dead, and the prophets testify that believers receive forgiveness through his name. While Peter speaks, the Holy Ghost falls on his hearers, who speak in tongues and glorify God. Astonished Jewish believers witness this gift to Gentiles, and Peter commands their baptism.

chapters.title: Gentile believers and the church at Antioch

parts.text: Believers in Jerusalem criticize Peter for entering an uncircumcised household and eating there. He recounts the vision, the Spirit’s direction, Cornelius’s angelic message, and the Holy Ghost falling on Gentile hearers as on the apostles at the beginning. Remembering Jesus’ promise, Peter asks how he could resist God, who gave them the same gift. His hearers stop objecting and glorify God for granting Gentiles repentance unto life.

Scattered believers bring the word to new regions, and preaching at Antioch produces many believers. Jerusalem sends Barnabas, who rejoices at God’s grace and urges steadfast faithfulness. He brings Saul from Tarsus, and they teach together for a year; the disciples are first called Christians there. Agabus predicts a widespread famine, and the believers send relief according to their means to Judea’s elders through Barnabas and Saul.

Herod kills James, John’s brother, and imprisons Peter under heavy guard. The church prays earnestly. An angel wakes Peter, releases his chains, and leads him past guards and through an opening iron gate. Peter realizes the deliverance is real and goes to the house where believers are praying. Rhoda recognizes his voice but, in her joy, leaves him outside while reporting it. The astonished group finally admits him, hears his account, and receives instructions to tell James and the brethren before he departs.

Herod unsuccessfully searches for Peter and orders the guards’ deaths. Later, while addressing people from Tyre and Sidon, he accepts praise as a god. An angel strikes him because he does not give God glory, and he dies. God’s word continues to grow. Barnabas and Saul return from their relief mission, bringing John Mark.

The Holy Ghost sets apart Barnabas and Saul, and the Antioch church sends them with prayer and fasting. In Cyprus, Saul, also called Paul, rebukes Elymas for opposing the gospel; temporary blindness falls on the sorcerer, and Sergius Paulus believes. John Mark leaves them at Perga. In Antioch in Pisidia, Paul recounts Israel’s history and proclaims Jesus, David’s promised descendant, crucified and raised in fulfilment of Scripture. Through him believers receive forgiveness and justification unavailable through Moses’ law.

On the next sabbath nearly the whole city gathers, provoking jealous opposition. Paul and Barnabas explain that the word had to come first to the Jews, but its rejection leads them to turn to Gentiles, according to God’s commission of light to the nations. Gentiles rejoice and believe, and the word spreads. Persecution drives the missionaries toward Iconium, while the disciples remain filled with joy and the Holy Ghost.

In Iconium, many Jews and Greeks believe while opponents stir division. Paul and Barnabas continue boldly with accompanying signs until a planned attack forces them to Lystra and Derbe. At Lystra, Paul heals a man lame from birth. The crowd mistakes the apostles for gods and prepares sacrifices. They tear their clothes and insist they are ordinary men, calling the people to turn from idols to the living Creator, whose goodness is witnessed in rain, fruitful seasons, and food.

Opponents arrive from Antioch and Iconium, persuade the crowd, and stone Paul, leaving him for dead. He rises and continues to Derbe. The missionaries then revisit the churches, strengthening disciples, warning that entry into God’s kingdom involves much tribulation, and appointing elders with prayer and fasting. Returning to Antioch, they report everything God has done, especially opening the door of faith to Gentiles.

chapters.title: The Jerusalem decision and a divided mission

parts.text: A dispute arises over teaching that Gentile believers must be circumcised to be saved. Paul and Barnabas take the question to Jerusalem. Peter recalls God’s gift of the Spirit to Gentiles and the cleansing of their hearts by faith, affirming salvation through Jesus’ grace for Jew and Gentile alike. After hearing the missionaries’ testimony, James cites the prophets and proposes not burdening Gentile converts, while asking them to abstain from idolatrous pollution, fornication, strangled meat, and blood.

The apostles, elders, and church send a confirming letter with Judas and Silas to Antioch, where it brings joy and encouragement. Later Paul proposes revisiting the churches. Barnabas wants to take John Mark, but Paul objects because he previously withdrew. Their disagreement separates them: Barnabas sails with Mark to Cyprus, and Paul takes Silas through Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches.

chapters.title: The call to Macedonia and the Philippian jailer

parts.text: Timotheus joins Paul, who circumcises him because local Jews know his father is Greek. The travellers deliver Jerusalem’s decisions and strengthen the churches. The Spirit prevents travel into certain regions, then Paul sees a Macedonian appealing for help. They cross to Macedonia and reach Philippi. By the river, the Lord opens Lydia’s heart to Paul’s message; she and her household are baptized, and she welcomes the missionaries into her home.

Paul casts a spirit of divination from a damsel, ending her masters’ hope of gain. They bring accusations, and Paul and Silas are beaten and imprisoned. As they pray and sing at midnight, an earthquake opens the prison. Paul stops the jailer from killing himself, and the missionaries proclaim salvation through faith in Jesus to his household. They believe, receive baptism, and show hospitality. Learning the prisoners are Roman citizens, the frightened magistrates personally escort them out.

In Thessalonica, Paul reasons from Scripture that Christ had to suffer and rise, and that Jesus is the Christ. Some believe, while jealous opponents stir a mob and accuse the missionaries of proclaiming another king. Paul and Silas leave for Berea, where hearers eagerly examine the Scriptures daily and many believe. Opponents from Thessalonica follow, prompting believers to send Paul to Athens while Silas and Timotheus remain.

Distressed by Athens’ idols, Paul reasons in synagogue and marketplace and is invited to explain his teaching at the Areopagus. Using an altar to the unknown God as his starting point, he proclaims the Creator who gives life, governs nations, and cannot be represented by crafted images. God now commands repentance because he has appointed judgment through the man he raised from the dead. Some mock resurrection, others defer judgment, and some believe.

At Corinth, Paul works as a tentmaker with Aquila and Priscilla and reasons in the synagogue. Opposition leads him to turn to Gentiles, while Crispus and many Corinthians believe and are baptized. The Lord encourages Paul in a vision to keep speaking, promising his presence; Paul teaches there for eighteen months. When opponents bring him before Gallio, the governor refuses to judge their religious dispute and dismisses them, ignoring the beating of Sosthenes.

Paul later sails with Aquila and Priscilla, briefly visits Ephesus, and continues toward Jerusalem and Antioch before strengthening disciples in Galatia and Phrygia. Apollos, an eloquent teacher well versed in Scripture but knowing only John’s baptism, arrives in Ephesus. Aquila and Priscilla explain God’s way more fully to him. Encouraged by the brethren, he goes to Achaia, greatly helping believers and publicly demonstrating from Scripture that Jesus is the Christ.

At Ephesus, Paul meets disciples knowing only John’s baptism, explains faith in Jesus, and baptizes them in his name. They receive the Holy Ghost through his laying on of hands. Paul teaches first in the synagogue, then daily in Tyrannus’s school, and the word reaches throughout Asia. God works extraordinary miracles through him. An evil spirit overpowers men attempting to use Jesus’ name without knowing him; fear spreads, believers confess their practices, and costly books of magic are burned.

Demetrius, a maker of silver shrines, rallies craftsmen whose trade is threatened by Paul’s rejection of handmade gods. They stir a riot in defence of Diana, seize Paul’s companions, and fill the theater with confusion. Friends prevent Paul from entering. The town clerk finally quiets the crowd, insists complaints belong in lawful courts, warns that the disturbance could bring charges, and dismisses the assembly.

Paul encourages believers through Macedonia and Greece, adjusting his return route because of a plot. At Troas, a gathering to break bread continues late as Paul speaks. Eutychus falls asleep in a window, falls three stories, and is taken up dead. Paul embraces him and announces that he lives; the young man is restored to the comforted believers. Paul continues his journey, hoping to reach Jerusalem by Pentecost.

From Miletus, Paul summons Ephesus’s elders and recalls his humble, tearful ministry and teaching of repentance toward God and faith in Jesus. Though imprisonment and affliction await, he intends to finish his course. He charges them to shepherd God’s purchased church and guard against false teachers from outside and within. Commending them to God and his word, he recalls his own labour and Jesus’ teaching that giving is more blessed than receiving. They pray and share a sorrowful farewell.

Paul travels toward Jerusalem, meeting disciples at Tyre who tell him through the Spirit not to go. At Cesarea, he stays with Philip, whose four daughters prophesy. Agabus uses Paul’s belt to predict that he will be bound and delivered to Gentiles. Though companions plead with him to stay, Paul declares himself ready even to die for Jesus’ name. They accept his determination and commit the outcome to the Lord’s will.

In Jerusalem, Paul reports the Gentile mission to James and the elders. To answer rumors about his attitude toward Jewish customs, he joins and supports four men completing a vow. Asian Jews nevertheless accuse him of opposing the people and temple and, wrongly assuming he brought Trophimus inside, provoke a violent mob. Roman soldiers rescue and bind him. After clarifying his identity to the commander, Paul receives permission to address the people in Hebrew.

Speaking in Hebrew, Paul describes his Jewish upbringing under Gamaliel and former zeal in persecuting believers. Near Damascus, a great light blinded him and Jesus identified himself as the one being persecuted. Ananias restored his sight and announced his appointment as a witness, calling him to baptism and to invoke the Lord’s name. Paul also recounts a later temple vision in which the Lord told him to leave Jerusalem and sent him far away to the Gentiles.

The crowd listens until his mention of the Gentiles, then demands his death. The commander orders examination by scourging, but Paul asks whether an uncondemned Roman citizen may legally be treated this way. The commander learns that Paul is a citizen by birth and becomes afraid over his treatment of him. The proposed interrogation stops, and the next day Paul is brought before the chief priests and council to clarify the accusations.

chapters.title: A promise of Rome and a plot exposed

parts.text: Before the council, Paul declares his clear conscience and rebukes an unlawful blow ordered by the high priest, then acknowledges Scripture’s prohibition against reviling a ruler. Recognizing the council’s division, he states that resurrection is the issue. Pharisees and Sadducees quarrel so violently that soldiers rescue him. That night the Lord encourages Paul: as he has testified in Jerusalem, he must also testify in Rome.

More than forty men vow not to eat or drink until they kill Paul and enlist leaders in requesting another hearing as cover for an ambush. Paul’s nephew learns of the plot and tells the commander. A substantial military escort takes Paul by night toward Cesarea, with a letter explaining the dispute and finding no capital offence. Governor Felix receives him and orders him held until his accusers arrive.

The high priest’s party, speaking through Tertullus, accuses Paul of stirring rebellion, leading the Nazarenes, and attempting to profane the temple. Paul denies causing any disturbance and points out that the accusations lack proof. He openly worships Israel’s God according to the way they call heresy, believes the law and prophets, and hopes in the resurrection of both just and unjust. He came with alms and offerings and was found purified in the temple; the original Asian accusers are absent.

Felix postpones judgment while allowing Paul’s friends to assist him. He and Drusilla later hear Paul discuss faith in Christ. Talk of righteousness, temperance, and judgment to come frightens Felix, who dismisses him for a more convenient time. Hoping for a bribe, Felix frequently speaks with Paul, yet leaves him imprisoned for two years and hands him over to Festus as a favour to the Jewish leaders.

When Festus visits Jerusalem, leaders ask that Paul be brought there, planning an ambush. Festus instead summons them to Cesarea. Their serious accusations remain unproved, and Paul denies wrongdoing against the law, temple, or Cesar. When Festus proposes a Jerusalem hearing, Paul insists on his right to Roman judgment. He is willing to die for a deserving offence but refuses to be handed over on false charges and appeals to Cesar. Festus grants the appeal.

King Agrippa and Bernice visit, and Festus explains that Paul’s case concerns religious disputes and Jesus, whom Paul says is alive. Agrippa asks to hear him. At a formal assembly, Festus states that he has found no capital offence but must send Paul because of the appeal. He hopes the examination will provide a definite account of charges to accompany the prisoner.

Paul explains that his trial concerns the hope promised to Israel’s fathers and asks why resurrection should seem incredible. Once a zealous Pharisee persecuting Jesus’ followers, he encountered the risen Jesus on the Damascus road. Jesus commissioned him to open people’s eyes, turn them from darkness and Satan to God, and bring forgiveness and an inheritance through faith. Paul obeyed, preaching repentance and fitting deeds among Jews and Gentiles. He says his message agrees with Moses and the prophets: Christ would suffer, rise, and bring light to both.

Festus interrupts, calling Paul mad, but Paul insists he speaks sober truth about publicly known events. He challenges Agrippa concerning belief in the prophets. Agrippa says Paul almost persuades him to be a Christian, and Paul wishes all his hearers shared his faith, though not his chains. The rulers agree he deserves neither death nor imprisonment and could have been released without his appeal to Cesar.

Paul sails toward Italy under Julius’s custody, receiving considerate treatment along the way. Contrary winds slow the voyage, and despite Paul’s warning, the ship leaves Crete in search of a better winter harbor. A violent storm drives them helplessly, forcing cargo and equipment overboard until hope is lost. Paul then encourages everyone: an angel has assured him that he must stand before Cesar and that all aboard will survive, although the ship will be lost and they will reach an island.

After fourteen nights, approaching land, sailors attempt to escape in the boat. At Paul’s warning, soldiers cut it loose. Paul gives thanks and urges everyone to eat. The ship runs aground and breaks apart; the centurion prevents soldiers from killing the prisoners because he wants to save Paul. All 276 aboard reach land safely, swimming or clinging to wreckage.

chapters.title: From Melita to witness in Rome

parts.text: The shipwrecked company receives kindness on Melita. A viper fastens to Paul’s hand, but he shakes it into the fire unharmed, overturning the islanders’ first assumption that he is a doomed murderer. Paul prays for and heals Publius’s father, and other sick islanders are healed. After three months, the travellers sail onward, meet believers in Italy, and reach Rome. Paul is permitted to live separately with a soldier guarding him.

Paul explains his imprisonment to local Jewish leaders and spends a full day teaching them about God’s kingdom and Jesus from the law and prophets. Some believe and others refuse. He cites Esaias’s warning about unresponsive hearts and declares that God’s salvation is sent to Gentiles who will hear. For two years, Paul welcomes visitors in his rented house and openly teaches about the Lord Jesus Christ without being forbidden.
